subject: Decision needed: Meridian on-ramp selection — Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Tom Willis <tom@meridian.ai>
To: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 22 May 2026 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Initial ask: Connectivity options for Project Meridian private deployment

Hi Monica,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. We are close to committing to Redwood Private for Project Meridian and need to pick an on-ramp pattern for connecting our VPCs/on-prem datacenter to your private deployment. High level constraints:
- Bulk inference traffic: ~1.2 Gbps sustained, spikes to 4–5 Gbps for batch jobs.
- Latency SLO: 50–100ms for online inference.
- Compliance: data at rest and in transit must remain within our control; audit logs are required.
- Timeline: pilot in 3 weeks, production in 10–12 weeks.

Can you summarize tradeoffs between VPC Peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN for our case? Also include any hybrid patterns that are production-proven. I've attached a simple network diagram and our requirements PDF.

Attachment: meridian_network_diagram.png (image)
Attachment: meridian_requirements.pdf (pdf)

Thanks,
Tom
CTO, Meridian AI

From: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Willis <tom@meridian.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 22 May 2026 11:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Initial ask: Connectivity options for Project Meridian private deployment

Tom —

Thanks for the clear context and the diagram. Short answer up top: all three options are viable, but the right pick depends on which of your constraints you prioritize (throughput vs. fine-grained access controls vs. speed to pilot). Below is a concise comparative summary; Ben will follow up with a bandwidth/latency estimate and engineering notes.

Quick guidance:
- If you need the lowest possible network hops and minimal per-request overhead inside the same cloud account/region: VPC Peering is attractive (low latency, no NAT).
- If you require tight service-level access controls (expose only inference ports, strong IAM-based acceptance) and cross-account/private-service semantics: PrivateLink is safer and easier to audit.
- If you have on-prem legacy gear or need an encrypted path across the public internet without a partner circuit: S2S VPN is the fastest to stand up for a pilot but watch throughput and jitter.

Recommended pilot: stand up an S2S VPN to validate functional behavior + PrivateLink for the control/management APIs. For production, lean toward PrivateLink for customer-sensitive traffic and either VPC Peering or Direct Connect/partner circuit for the high-throughput data plane.

Next steps: Ben, can you add a short technical note (bandwidth/ENI limits/cost) and any DE/ops playbook items? I will loop in Security and Procurement once we pick a path.

— Monica
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>, Tom Willis <tom@meridian.ai>
Cc: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 22 May 2026 15:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Initial ask: Connectivity options for Project Meridian private deployment — technical note

Tom / Monica —

I dug into the traffic profile and sketched practical limits & tradeoffs. TL;DR: for 1–5 Gbps sustained with low p99 latency we recommend either peering within the same cloud region (if Meridian's VPC is in the same account/region) or a dedicated partner interconnect (Direct Connect / Cloud Interconnect). PrivateLink will work but has some operational knobs to watch for at high throughput. S2S VPN is fine for pilot only.

Notes:
- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Lowest added latency; routing is simple (routes + security groups); no additional gateway hops.
  - Cons: Peering is non-transitive; cross-account peering requires acceptance and careful route table hygiene; scaling across many accounts/regions becomes operationally heavy.
  - Perf: can easily carry multi-Gbps if both sides have proper ENIs and instance throughput; watch for IP CIDR overlap.

- PrivateLink (AWS Interface Endpoints / Endpoint Service)
  - Pros: Fine-grained service exposure (you publish a specific endpoint for inference); works across accounts; strong vector for least-privilege networking and auditing.
  - Cons: Endpoint ENI scaling — each ENI has throughput limits; throughput per endpoint depends on instance types and NLBs behind the service. Slight extra latency (single-digit ms) vs peering. Egress pricing and per-hour ENI costs can add up.
  - Operational: You must run a service fronted by an NLB or Gateway Load Balancer. For high throughput we recommend autoscaled NLB workers and sticky connection handling where appropriate.

- Site-to-Site VPN
  - Pros: Quick to provision for pilots; encrypted over public internet; common for on-prem customers.
  - Cons: Typically higher latency/jitter and lower throughput than wired/private circuits. Need HA pairs; MTU and fragmentation issues may appear with large payloads.
  - Perf: Achievable 1–2 Gbps with software ASA/edge boxes but requires big iron or multiple tunnels for >3 Gbps.

Hybrid options we use in production:
- PrivateLink for control plane & admin APIs + Peering/Direct Connect for bulk dataplane. This gives least-privilege access to management surfaces while preserving throughput.
- Start pilot with S2S VPN to validate application-level behavior, then migrate dataplane to peering/direct connect and management to PrivateLink.

Implementation checklist (short):
- Verify CIDR non-overlap or plan NATing for peering.
- Define security group + NACL templates for inference endpoints.
- Plan endpoint scaling (NLB + worker pool) for PrivateLink; estimate ENI counts by peak conn.
- If using VPN: plan HA tunnels, BGP vs static routes, and MTU testing.
- Instrumentation: ensure per-route latency/cost metrics in Redwood Console; add KV-cache affinity considerations.

I'll attach a quick cost/throughput spreadsheet and an internal runbook excerpt for PrivateLink scale patterns.

Attachments in this message: cost_comparison_estimate.xlsx (spreadsheet)

— Ben
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial ask: Connectivity options for Project Meridian private deployment

Ben, Monica —

Helpful notes, thank you. A few clarifications from our side:
- We control a VPC in the same cloud provider and region as Redwood's planned datacenter, but it's in a different account.
- On-prem is primarily for backups/secondary batch jobs; most online inference traffic will originate from our VPC.
- Compliance team prefers a pattern where control plane calls are individually auditable and access-limited; they also prefer not to expose whole VPC peering that could allow lateral access.

Given that: PrivateLink for control with a peering/dataplane interconnect for bulk inference sounds logical. Can you outline required changes on our side (route tables, IAM, expected ENI counts)? I'll pull in our network engineer if needed.

Tom

From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Willis <tom@meridian.ai>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 24 May 2026 09:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Initial ask: Connectivity options for Project Meridian private deployment — recommended plan

Team —

Picking up from Ben's analysis and Tom's clarifications: here is a recommended plan we have delivered to similar customers (summary + explicit action items).

Recommended topology (PHASED):
Phase 0 (pilot, 2–3 weeks):
- Stand up S2S VPN between Meridian on-prem and Redwood Private to validate auth, telemetry, and basic routing.
- Configure PrivateLink endpoint service for management APIs (audit-friendly).
- Monitor latencies and validate p99.

Phase 1 (production baseline, 6–12 weeks):
- Create an AWS VPC Peering connection between Meridian VPC and Redwood's dedicated VPC for data plane traffic (same region, cross-account).
- Publish control-plane endpoints via PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to Meridian account only.
- Harden security groups: restrict to specific ports (inference ports + health checks) and enforce least-privilege IAM for management endpoints.
- Optional: for >5 Gbps or multi-region, add a Direct Connect / partner circuit and route dataplane over that.

Detailed action items for Meridian (what you need to configure):
- Accept cross-account VPC peering and add route table entries pointing inference subnets to the peering connection.
- Reserve / allocate subnets for interface endpoints (PrivateLink) and ensure enough IP capacity for ENIs. Estimate: 1–2 ENIs per AZ per 1.5 Gbps of sustained throughput behind the NLB; we will refine after pilot telemetry.
- Prepare security contact and provide ASN if using BGP for Direct Connect/VPN.
- Update ACLs and firewall rules to allow health probes from Redwood NLB IPs; we'll provide exact CIDR ranges.

Security & compliance notes:
- PrivateLink provides strong surface-area reduction for management traffic; peering exposes routing-level connectivity so limit which subnets are peered and use restrictive NACLs.
- We'll enable per-request logging for control endpoints and hand over audit logs for SOC / compliance.

Tentative schedule:
- Pilot S2S VPN + PrivateLink control endpoints: target start 2026-06-07.
- Production peering + scaled NLBs: target cutover 2026-07-15 (tentative, dependent on procurement).

I'll follow up with a short checklist for your network team and a sample CloudFormation snippet for endpoint creation.

— Soojin
Principal Network Architect, Redwood Inference

3) Security review: Redwood Security + Meridian Compliance — complete MCP security questionnaire and agree on audit log retention. Attached: mcp_security_questionnaire.pdf
4) Procurement: Meridian Procurement + Redwood Sales — review cost_comparison_estimate.xlsx and confirm ROI/commitment model. (Owner: Procurement teams)
